lessons.title: Start here · How this pack works

blocks.text: The SAFe DevOps Practitioner exam, SDP 6.0, has 45 single-select multiple-choice questions and a 90-minute timer. The pass mark is 73%, which means 33 correct answers. It is web-based and closed book, and unanswered questions count as wrong. The first two attempts are included when taken within 60 days of finishing the course. These facts come from the exam study guide as it stood on 14 November 2026. Check the guide again before you sit the exam.
blocks.title: The exam

blocks.text: Mocks draw from each domain in proportion to the midpoint of its range. Each domain has one lesson.
blocks.title: Exam domains and this pack

blocks.text:
Read the lessons in order; each objective unlocks the next. After a lesson, practise that domain in learning mode, where every answer is explained. Short mocks have 20 questions in 40 minutes, and full mocks match the real exam at 45 questions in 90 minutes.

If you want a placement check, take the first short mock in learning mode before reading anything. Treat the result as a rough signal of where to start, not as a measure of ability.

Readiness in this pack asks for more than 90% on recent mocks, a deliberate margin above the real 73% pass mark. Readiness and mastery are practice signals. They are not predictions of your exam result.
blocks.title: How to use the pack

blocks.text:
Almost every question sits somewhere on one picture: four aspects, each with four activities.

Continuous Exploration: hypothesize, collaborate and research, architect, synthesize.
Continuous Integration: develop, build, test end-to-end, stage.
Continuous Deployment: deploy, verify, monitor, respond.
Release on Demand: release, stabilize, measure, learn.

If you can place a practice in the right activity, you can answer most recall questions. Learn the sixteen names in order.

lessons.title: 1 · Introducing DevOps
lessons.summary: The problem DevOps solves, CALMR, and the pipeline at a glance.

blocks.text:
In many organisations the people who build a solution and the people who run it are measured on opposite things. Development is rewarded for change. Operations is rewarded for stability. Work crosses a wall between them in large batches, releases are rare and painful, and each failure makes the next release rarer.

SAFe defines DevOps as a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that support the integration, automation and collaboration needed to develop and operate a solution. It bridges the gap between those who build and those who support and maintain. Its goal is to deliver value whenever there is a business need.

Notice what the definition leaves out. DevOps is not a team, a job title or a tool.
blocks.title: The problem to be solved

blocks.text:
CALMR is the mindset behind SAFe DevOps. It guides the train toward continuous value delivery through five elements.

Culture: shared responsibility for the whole value stream, and learning from failure without blame.
Automation: removing manual steps from the pipeline.
Lean flow: small batches, limits on work in process, short queues.
Measurement: data on flow, quality and value.
Recovery: designing and rehearsing for fast restoration of service.

The older industry model was CALMS, with sharing as the last letter. SAFe treats sharing as part of culture and gives the fifth place to recovery.

Two more ideas run through the course. Continuous testing means tests are automated and run all the time, not in a phase at the end. Continuous security means security practices are built into each stage.
blocks.title: CALMR

blocks.text:
Norrland Rail releases its ticketing system four times a year. Each release takes a weekend, and the last one was rolled back.

A CALMR reading: the culture rewards developers for features and operations for uptime, so each side protects itself. Deployments are manual, so automation is low. Four releases a year means very large batches, the opposite of lean flow. Nobody can say how long a change takes to reach customers, so measurement is missing. The rollback took nine hours, so recovery is weak.

The first step is not a tool purchase. It is to bring both groups together to map the value stream, which is the next lesson.
blocks.title: Worked example · Norrland Rail

blocks.text:
Generic answer: create a DevOps team to own deployments. SAFe answer: DevOps is a shared mindset and set of practices across the train; a separate team is another handoff.

Generic answer: deploy less often to reduce risk. SAFe answer: deploy smaller changes more often, so each one carries less risk.

Wrong level: CALMR is the mindset. It is not a practice domain, a pipeline stage or a metric set.

Wrong letter: the R is recovery, not release or resilience.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Take a recent release you know. Write one sentence for each CALMR element describing what you observed. Circle the weakest element and write one small change that would improve it within a month.

lessons.title: 2 · Value Stream Mapping
lessons.summary: Why and how to map a value stream, and the metrics that show its health.

blocks.text:
A value stream is the series of steps that turns a trigger, such as a customer request, into delivered value. Mapping it makes the steps, handoffs and delays visible to everyone at once. The map describes the system. It is not a tool for rating people or teams.

The people who do the work build the map together: business, product, development, testing, security and operations. A map drawn by one group misses the delays that happen before and after its own steps.
blocks.title: Why map

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of value stream mapping; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Time someone is actively working on the item
Elapsed time for the step, including waiting
Share of output the next step can use without rework
blocks.title: Three measures on each step

blocks.text:
Add the process times and the lead times along the stream. Process time divided by lead time is the activity ratio, which SAFe's flow metrics call flow efficiency: time in value-adding work divided by total flow time. In most organisations it is surprisingly low, because work waits far longer than it is worked on.

Multiply the percent complete and accurate values to get the rolled value. Three steps at 80, 50 and 50 percent give 20 percent: only one item in five passes through without rework.

The largest improvement usually sits in the delays between steps. After the current state is understood, the group designs a future state and an improvement backlog.
blocks.title: Reading the totals

blocks.text:
SAFe names six flow metrics. Flow time is the time from start to completion of an item. Flow velocity is the number of items completed in a period. Flow load is the number of items in progress. Flow efficiency is active time divided by total flow time. Flow distribution is the mix of item types. Flow predictability is how consistently commitments are met.

Measure and Grow uses three measurement domains: outcomes, flow and competency. Outcomes ask whether solutions meet customer and business needs. Flow asks how efficiently value is delivered. Competency asks how proficient the organisation is in the practices.
blocks.title: Flow metrics and Measure and Grow

blocks.text:
Calder Freight maps the path of a feature. Development takes 5 days of work inside 12 days elapsed. Testing takes 2 days of work, after 11 days waiting for an environment. Deployment takes half a day of work, after 20 days waiting for a monthly window.

Total process time is 7.5 days and total lead time is 45.5 days, so flow efficiency is about 16 percent. Making developers faster would touch 5 days. Removing the wait for an environment and the monthly window would touch 31. The improvement backlog starts with self-service environments and automated deployment.
blocks.title: Worked example · Calder Freight

blocks.text:
Generic answer: find the slowest team and speed it up. SAFe answer: look at the waits between steps, which no single team owns.

A manager deciding alone: a map drawn by managers without the people who do the work is a guess.

Wrong metric: flow load counts items in progress; flow velocity counts items finished. Rising load with flat velocity means longer flow time.

Wrong reading: percent complete and accurate is about the quality of the handoff, not progress against scope.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Sketch four to six steps from idea to production for something you delivered recently. Estimate process time and lead time for each. Compute flow efficiency. Mark the single longest wait and name who would need to be in the room to remove it.

lessons.title: 3 · Continuous Exploration
lessons.summary: Hypotheses, research, architecture for delivery, and synthesis into a prioritised backlog.

blocks.text:
Continuous Exploration is the first aspect of the pipeline and the largest exam domain. It drives innovation and alignment on what to build by continually exploring market and customer needs, and it produces a vision, a roadmap and a set of features in the ART Backlog. Product Management prioritises those features.

It replaces a large up-front requirements phase with a steady flow of small features. Every idea is treated as a hypothesis until evidence supports it.
blocks.title: What exploration is for

blocks.text: The activity names follow the topic list in the study guide; the descriptions are the author's.
rows: State the expected, measurable benefit and how it will be tested
Work with customers and stakeholders to understand needs
Shape the solution so it can be delivered continuously
Turn the result into a vision, roadmap and prioritised features
blocks.title: The four activities

blocks.text:
A benefit hypothesis is the proposed measurable benefit of an epic, capability, feature or story. For a large initiative, a Minimum Viable Product is an early and minimal version used to prove or disprove the epic hypothesis. Lean startup thinking then asks for a decision: persevere, pivot or stop. Innovation accounting supplies the leading indicators that make that decision possible before financial results arrive.

Research is primary when you gather evidence first-hand, for example by watching users work, and secondary when you rely on reports and data collected by others. Lean UX keeps the design loop short by focusing on iterative learning and customer outcomes.
blocks.title: Hypothesize, then research

blocks.text:
The pipeline can only flow if the solution is designed for it. The Architectural Runway is the existing code, components and technical infrastructure needed to implement near-term features with minimal redesign. Emergent design alone does not scale, so SAFe balances it with intentional architecture. Enablers pave the runway and come in four types: exploration, architecture, infrastructure and compliance.

Architects design for releasability, so that deployment can be separated from release, for testability, for operations and for security. Threat modelling belongs here, before code exists. Nonfunctional requirements are system qualities that constrain the backlogs and are revisited with the definition of done.
blocks.title: Architect for continuous delivery

blocks.text:
A feature delivers business value and fits in one planning interval for one train. It carries a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria. The backlog is sequenced by Weighted Shortest Job First: cost of delay divided by job size. Cost of delay adds user and business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement.

WSJF applies to the whole backlog. A pipeline enabler that removes delay from every later feature can outrank a customer feature.
blocks.title: Synthesize and prioritise

blocks.text:
Solace Health believes online booking will cut missed appointments. The hypothesis: clinics using the new flow will see missed appointments fall by a fifth within three months. The leading indicator is the share of bookings made online each week.

Product Management visits three clinics and watches reception staff. Architects decide the booking service must be deployable on its own and hidden behind a toggle. The feature set is written with benefit hypotheses, scored with WSJF and brought to PI Planning. If clinics do not use the flow, the result is a pivot, not a larger budget.
blocks.title: Worked example · Solace Health

blocks.text:
Generic answer: a customer request is a requirement. SAFe answer: it is a hypothesis to validate.

Generic answer: the MVP is the smallest sellable release. SAFe answer: it is the smallest thing that tests the epic hypothesis.

Wrong role: Product Management prioritises features in the ART Backlog; the Product Owner owns the team backlog.

Wrong place: designing for separate deployment and release is an exploration decision, made by architects, not something bolted on at deployment time.

Enablers are not overhead to be scheduled last; they compete on WSJF like everything else.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Pick one feature you know. Write its benefit hypothesis in one sentence with a number in it. Name one leading indicator you could read within two weeks of release. Then score it and one enabler from 1 to 10 on the three cost of delay parts and on size, and see which wins.

lessons.title: 4 · Continuous Integration
lessons.summary: Develop, build, test end-to-end and stage, with the practices that keep the trunk healthy.

blocks.text:
Continuous Integration is the aspect of the pipeline where new functionality is developed, tested, integrated and validated in preparation for deployment and release. The aim is a system that is always running and potentially deployable, even in the middle of development.

It has four activities. Develop implements stories and commits code and components to version control. Build creates deployable binaries and merges development branches into the trunk. Test end-to-end validates the solution. Stage hosts and validates it in a staging environment before production.
blocks.title: What integration is for

blocks.text: The activity names are from the public article; the practices are written from the author's knowledge.
rows: Small stories, TDD, BDD, version control, built-in quality
Trunk-based development, gated commits, build automation, security scanning
Test automation, production-like environments, test data, service virtualisation, NFR testing
Staging environment, blue-green deployment, System Demo
blocks.title: Practices by activity

blocks.text:
Test-Driven Development builds and runs a test before the code it checks. Behavior-Driven Development defines business-facing scenarios before or with the specification of behaviour, and needs three perspectives: customer, development and test. Both are test-first practices. Together they produce many fast automated tests and few slow end-to-end ones.

Quality is the whole team's job. Agile testing is collaborative, and tests are automated wherever possible.
blocks.title: Test-first

blocks.text:
# Illustrative pipeline definition. It is displayed here, not run.
trigger:
  branches: [main]            # trunk-based: every merge to main starts the pipeline

stages:
  - stage: Build              # CI: build
    steps:
      - script: dotnet build --configuration Release
      - script: dotnet test tests/Unit        # fast developer tests
      - script: security-scan ./src           # static analysis on each commit
  - stage: TestEndToEnd       # CI: test end-to-end
    steps:
      - script: deploy --env test --version $(Build.Id)
      - script: dotnet test tests/Acceptance  # BDD scenarios, virtualised partners
  - stage: Stage              # CI: stage
    steps:
      - script: deploy --env staging --slot green --version $(Build.Id)
  - stage: Deploy             # CD: deploy and verify
    steps:
      - script: deploy --env production --toggles off --version $(Build.Id)
      - script: dotnet test tests/Smoke --env production
blocks.title: A short pipeline example

blocks.text:
Teams at Farrow Systems keep feature branches for three weeks. Merges fail, and the main line is broken for days before each System Demo.

The train moves to short-lived branches merged daily, with a gated commit that runs the build and unit tests before a change reaches the trunk. A partner's payment service is rarely available in test, so the team virtualises it. The staging environment is rebuilt from the same definitions as production, and the System Demo runs from staging each iteration.
blocks.title: Worked example · Farrow Systems

blocks.text:
Generic answer: the System Team integrates for everyone. SAFe answer: teams integrate continuously; the System Team supports the infrastructure.

Generic answer: testers own quality. SAFe answer: the whole team does.

Wrong activity: merging to the trunk is build, not develop. Hosting in a production-like environment is stage, not deploy.

Wrong event: the integrated work of the whole train is shown at the System Demo each iteration, not only at Inspect and Adapt.

TDD versus BDD: TDD is the developer cycle on units of code; BDD is shared, business-facing behaviour.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Look at the pipeline example. For each step, name the integration activity it belongs to. Then mark the one step your own pipeline lacks or runs by hand, and write what it would take to automate it.

lessons.title: 5 · Continuous Deployment
lessons.summary: Deploy, verify, monitor and respond, and why deployment is separate from release.

blocks.text:
Continuous Deployment is the aspect of the pipeline that automates the migration of new functionality from a staging environment to production, where it is made available for release. Deployment is a technical event. Release is a business decision. Keeping them apart is the central idea of this domain.

When deployment is separate from release, changes reach production without altering what users see. That allows functionality to be shown to chosen customers, experiments such as A/B tests, small batches, and release when the business wants it. Automation lowers the transaction cost of each deployment, which is what makes small batches economical.
blocks.title: What deployment is for

blocks.text: Activity names and meanings are from the public article; the practices are written from the author's knowledge.
rows: Deployment automation, feature toggles, dark launches, selective and self-service deployment
Confirm it works in production before customers see it
Production testing, test automation, NFR tests
Watch production and report on issues
Proactive detection, rollback and fix forward, immutable infrastructure, blameless reviews
blocks.title: The four activities

blocks.text:
A feature toggle hides deployed code until it is switched on. A dark launch runs functionality in production without users seeing it. A canary release shows a change to a small share of real users and widens gradually; it is a release technique. Blue-green deployment keeps two production environments and switches traffic between them.

When something fails, restoring service comes first. Roll back when that is fastest and safe; fix forward when a fix is quicker or rollback is not possible.
blocks.title: Techniques that are easy to confuse

blocks.text:
# Illustrative. Deployment puts code in production; the toggle decides who sees it.
deploy:
  environment: production
  strategy: blue-green
  toggles:
    new-pricing-engine: off        # deployed, verified, not released
verify:
  - smoke-tests --env production
  - nfr-check --latency-p95 300ms
monitor:
  alerts:
    error-rate: "> 1% for 5m -> page on-call, auto-rollback"
blocks.title: Toggle-guarded deployment

blocks.text:
Garnet Travel deploys a new search service at ten in the morning with its toggle off. Smoke tests pass in production. The toggle is opened to staff, and telemetry shows response times within the agreed limit.

A later deployment raises the error rate for a tenth of users. The pipeline rolls back in two minutes. The review asks what allowed the fault through and adds a production test; it does not ask who typed the command.
blocks.title: Worked example · Garnet Travel

blocks.text:
Generic answer: deployed means released. SAFe answer: deployed means in production and available for release.

Wrong aspect: monitor and respond belong to Continuous Deployment. Stabilize, which sounds similar, belongs to Release on Demand.

A manager deciding: a change board that approves each deployment adds delay and no information. Automation and verification provide the control.

Canary versus dark launch: users see a canary; they do not see a dark launch.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

lessons.title: 6 · Release on Demand
lessons.summary: Release, stabilize, measure and learn, and who decides when to release.

blocks.text:
Release on Demand is the aspect of the pipeline that releases new functionality immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs. On demand does not mean constantly. It means the business can release whenever it chooses, which for one solution is many times a day and for another is twice a year.

Product Management and the business owners decide when to release, which features, and to which users. Market rhythms and roadmap milestones inform the timing. Because release is decoupled from deployment, marketing can plan promotions and sales can schedule with confidence.
blocks.title: What release on demand means

blocks.text: The activity names follow the study guide's topic list; the practices are written from the author's knowledge.
rows: Feature toggles, canary releases, decoupled release elements
Keep the solution reliable, secure and available
Failover and disaster recovery, continuous security monitoring, architecting for operations
Compare results with the benefit hypothesis
Decide what to do next and improve the pipeline
Lean startup thinking, value stream mapping, relentless improvement
blocks.title: The four activities

blocks.text:
Measure asks whether the released functionality produced the benefit that was predicted in exploration. Passing acceptance tests shows the feature was built as specified. It does not show the feature was worth building.

Learn turns the evidence into a decision to persevere, pivot or stop, and into improvements to the pipeline. What is learned feeds back into Continuous Exploration, which makes the pipeline a loop.
blocks.title: Closing the loop

blocks.text:
Halyard Retail deploys a loyalty feature in September behind a toggle. Marketing wants to launch with a November campaign, so the feature stays deployed and dark. In November it opens to two percent of customers as a canary, then to everyone.

The hypothesis was a rise in repeat purchases. After four weeks the leading indicator, the share of customers who open the loyalty page twice, has not moved. Product Management pivots the feature toward a simpler reward and records the learning as input to the next exploration cycle.
blocks.title: Worked example · Halyard Retail

blocks.text:
Generic answer: release when the code is ready. SAFe answer: release when the business needs it.

Wrong role: the Release Train Engineer and the teams make release routine; Product Management and business owners choose the timing.

Wrong cadence: the planning interval is a planning cadence. It does not fix when releases happen.

Wrong meaning of stabilize: it is not a hardening phase for unfinished testing.

Monolith thinking: releasing every element together at the pace of the slowest one. SAFe decouples release elements.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer
