questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe DevOps?

options.text: A toolchain that replaces manual release approvals
A phase that follows development and testing
A mindset, culture and set of technical practices
A team that owns deployments for the whole train

questions.explanation: SAFe defines DevOps as a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that support integration, automation and collaboration. Treating it as a separate team recreates the handoff between builders and operators that DevOps exists to remove.

questions.prompt: What does the R in CALMR stand for?

options.text: Recovery
Release
Resilience
Reporting

questions.explanation: CALMR is culture, automation, lean flow, measurement and recovery. Release is tempting because the pipeline ends with Release on Demand, but the mindset names the ability to recover from failure.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe use recovery where the older CALMS model had sharing?

options.text: Sharing applies to operations and leaves out developers
Sharing was replaced by measurement of flow
Sharing is treated as a natural part of culture
Sharing slows teams that work in small batches

questions.explanation: The CALMR article explains that sharing already belongs to culture, so the fifth element is given to recovery. Sharing is still expected; it has moved, it has not been dropped.

questions.prompt: At Norrland Rail, developers are rewarded for shipping features and operations staff are rewarded for uptime, and each group blames the other after a failed release. Which problem does DevOps address here?

options.text: The gap between those who build and those who run the solution
The absence of a single manager for both departments
The shortage of specialist testers inside the operations group
The missing sign-off stage before each production release

questions.explanation: SAFe says DevOps bridges the gap between the people who build solutions and the people who support and maintain them. Adding a sign-off stage widens the gap, because it adds another handoff and delay.

questions.prompt: A train at Halden Insurance has automated its builds and deployments, yet failed releases still lead to a search for the person at fault. Which CALMR element needs the most attention?

options.text: Lean flow
Culture
Measurement
Automation

questions.explanation: A culture of shared responsibility treats failure as something the system produced and the group learns from. Automation is already in place here, so more tooling would leave the blame habit untouched.

questions.prompt: A team at Brightwater Bank works on fourteen features at once and finishes few of them. Which CALMR element speaks most directly to this?

options.text: Culture
Lean flow
Measurement
Recovery

questions.explanation: Lean flow covers limiting work in process, reducing batch size and managing queue lengths. Measurement would show the problem, but the remedy is to limit how much is started.

questions.prompt: Leaders at Corvane Logistics want proof that their DevOps investment is working. Which outcome would the CALMR approach point to?

options.text: A shorter mean time to recover after incidents
A higher share of staff holding tool certificates
A longer stabilisation period before each release
A larger number of approval steps completed per release

questions.explanation: Improved mean time to recover is one of the outcomes the CALMR article lists, with faster time to market and fewer defects. More approval steps measure activity in the process, and they slow delivery.

questions.prompt: What does continuous security mean in SAFe DevOps?

options.text: Security testing moves to a hardening iteration
Security work is built into each stage of the pipeline
Security staff review the solution once before release
Security is the duty of the operations group alone

questions.explanation: Continuous security, often called DevSecOps, places security practices such as threat modelling and automated scanning throughout the pipeline. A single review before release finds problems when they are most expensive to fix.

questions.prompt: A train at Meridian Health runs most checks by hand in the last week of each planning interval. Which step fits continuous testing?

options.text: Reduce testing to the features marked as high risk
Automate tests and run them as each change is integrated
Add a second manual test cycle after the release
Move all testing to a separate quality department before release

questions.explanation: Agile testing in SAFe builds quality in with tests that are automated wherever possible and run continuously. A second manual cycle adds delay and still finds defects late.

questions.prompt: Which four aspects make up the Continuous Delivery Pipeline, in order?

options.text: Exploration, development, staging, deployment
Planning, development, testing, release management
Integration, exploration, release on demand, deployment
Exploration, integration, deployment, release on demand

questions.explanation: The pipeline runs from Continuous Exploration through Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment to Release on Demand. The second option uses the right names in the wrong order; deployment comes before release.

questions.prompt: A product at Aster Mobility has a mobile app that could ship daily and a vehicle unit that ships twice a year. What does SAFe suggest?

options.text: Decouple the parts so each releases at its own cadence
Ship the vehicle unit daily to match the app
Hold the app so both parts ship in the same release
Release both parts at the end of each planning interval

questions.explanation: The pipeline article says continuous can mean different things for different parts, and that decoupling avoids one monolithic release. Holding the app delays value that customers could already use.

questions.prompt: Who builds and manages the Continuous Delivery Pipeline?

options.text: The System Team on behalf of the business owners
Each Agile team separately for its own stories
The Agile Release Train itself, alone or shared
A central release department outside the trains

questions.explanation: SAFe says each Agile Release Train builds and manages, or shares, a pipeline so it can deliver value independently. A central release department takes that independence away and adds a handoff.

questions.prompt: According to SAFe, what is the goal of DevOps?

options.text: To remove the operations role from the train
To deploy each commit to the whole customer base at once
To deliver value whenever there is a business need
To reach full automation of the manual tasks

questions.explanation: The DevOps article states the goal as delivering value at any time there is a business need. Deploying each commit to all customers confuses deployment with release, which SAFe keeps separate.

questions.prompt: A coach at Tallis Energy lists CALMR as one of the technical practice domains of DevOps. What is wrong with that?

options.text: CALMR is the mindset that guides the practice domains
CALMR applies to portfolios, and practice domains to teams
CALMR is the pipeline, and practice domains are its stages
CALMR is a metric set, and practice domains are roles

questions.explanation: SAFe presents CALMR as the mindset behind DevOps and the practice domains as what enables the pipeline. Calling CALMR the pipeline mixes up the mindset with the four pipeline aspects.

questions.prompt: A train at Verity Foods deploys once a quarter and each deployment takes a weekend of manual work. Which reasoning matches the DevOps view?

options.text: Add reviewers so each quarterly deployment is safer
Freeze development earlier to give operations more time
Deploy less often so there are fewer risky weekends
Deploy smaller changes more often so each one carries less risk

questions.explanation: Small, frequent, automated deployments lower the risk and cost of each change and speed up learning. Deploying less often makes each batch bigger, which raises the risk it was meant to reduce.

questions.prompt: After an outage at Lumen Travel, the team restored service in ten minutes because it had rehearsed a rollback. Which CALMR element does this show?

options.text: Automation
Measurement
Lean flow
Recovery

questions.explanation: Recovery is about designing and practising for failure so service returns quickly. Automation may have helped, but the rehearsed ability to restore service is what the scenario describes.

questions.prompt: Match each CALMR element to what it stresses.

options.text: Removing manual steps from the pipeline
Data on flow, quality and value
A separate team that owns releases
Small batches and limits on work in process
Shared responsibility across the value stream
Fast restoration of service after failure

questions.explanation: The five elements are culture, automation, lean flow, measurement and recovery. A separate release team is the opposite of shared responsibility and belongs to none of them.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of mapping a value stream?

options.text: To document the tools used at each step
To compare the output of individual team members
To see how work flows and where it waits
To record who is accountable for each defect

questions.explanation: A value stream map makes the steps, handoffs and delays visible so the group can decide what to improve. It looks at the system; using it to rate people destroys the trust the exercise needs.

questions.prompt: In value stream mapping, what is process time?

options.text: The elapsed time from the request to its delivery
The time someone is actively working on the item in a step
The time an item waits before a step picks it up
The time needed to repair work returned by a later step

questions.explanation: Process time counts active work on the item. The first distractor describes total lead time, which includes all the waiting.

questions.prompt: What does percent complete and accurate tell you about a step?

options.text: How much of the scope planned for the step has been finished
How much of its capacity is used
How many of its automated tests are passing
How much of its output the next step can use without rework

questions.explanation: Percent complete and accurate is a quality measure of the handoff: the share of work the next step receives in a usable state. It is easy to confuse with progress against scope, which says nothing about rework.

questions.prompt: A map at Orchard Retail shows total process time of 6 days and total lead time of 60 days. What is the flow efficiency?

options.text: 90 percent
54 percent
6 percent
10 percent

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency is the time spent in value-adding work divided by total flow time, so 6 divided by 60 is 10 percent. The 90 percent figure is the share of time spent waiting.

questions.prompt: Three steps in a map at Pine Harbor have percent complete and accurate values of 80, 50 and 50. What is the rolled value for the stream?

options.text: 50 percent
60 percent
180 percent
20 percent

questions.explanation: The rolled value multiplies the steps: 0.8 times 0.5 times 0.5 is 0.2. The average of 60 percent is tempting, but it hides how rework compounds along the stream.

questions.prompt: A map at Calder Freight shows that work spends two days in testing and eleven days waiting for a test environment. Where should the group look first?

options.text: At the number of test cases per story
At the wait for the environment
At the speed of the testers
At the size of the test environment

questions.explanation: Delays between steps are usually much larger than the active work, so removing the wait gives the bigger gain. Making testers faster would save part of two days and leave eleven untouched.

questions.prompt: Who should take part in a value stream mapping workshop?

options.text: People who do the work at each step, from concept to cash
The managers of each department, without their staff
The developers alone, since the code is theirs
An external auditor who interviews teams afterwards

questions.explanation: The map is accurate when people from every step build it together, including business, development, security and operations. A developers-only map misses the delays before and after development.

questions.prompt: A group at Fennel Bank has drawn its current state map. What comes next?

options.text: Repeat the mapping of the current state with a different facilitator
Assign each delay on the map to the manager responsible for that step
Design a future state and agree the improvements that move toward it
File the current state map as evidence for the next audit

questions.explanation: The current state is the baseline; its value comes from the future state and the improvement items that follow. Assigning delays to managers turns a system view into blame.

questions.prompt: Which flow metric counts the work items currently in progress?

options.text: Flow load
Flow time
Flow distribution
Flow velocity

questions.explanation: Flow load is the number of items in the system, active or waiting. Flow velocity counts items completed in a period, which is throughput.

questions.prompt: Which flow metric shows the proportion of work by type, such as features, enablers and defects?

options.text: Flow distribution
Flow load
Flow efficiency
Flow predictability

questions.explanation: Flow distribution shows the mix of item types in the system. Flow load counts how many items there are, whatever their type.

questions.prompt: Features at Quarry Media take 70 days from start to completion, and leaders ask which metric tracks this. Which is it?

options.text: Flow load
Flow time
Flow predictability
Flow velocity

questions.explanation: Flow time is the elapsed time from the start to the completion of a work item. Flow velocity would say how many features finish, not how long each takes.

questions.prompt: Flow load at Stonebridge Telecom keeps rising while flow velocity stays flat. What is the likely effect?

options.text: Flow time will grow because more work waits in queues
Flow time will shrink because more work is under way
Flow efficiency will rise because people stay busy
Flow predictability will improve as the backlog grows

questions.explanation: When more work is started than finished, queues lengthen and each item takes longer. Being busy is not the same as flowing; a full system has more waiting, so efficiency falls.

questions.prompt: Which three measurement domains does SAFe use in Measure and Grow?

options.text: Scope, schedule and cost
Velocity, quality and morale
Culture, automation and recovery
Outcomes, flow and competency

questions.explanation: Measure and Grow evaluates outcomes, flow and competency. Scope, schedule and cost is the project triangle, which says little about whether value reaches customers.

questions.prompt: A portfolio at Tern Aviation wants to know whether its solutions meet customer needs. Which measurement domain answers that?

options.text: Competency
Capacity
Outcomes
Flow

questions.explanation: Outcomes ask whether solutions meet customer and business needs, using indicators such as KPIs and OKRs. Flow asks how efficiently value is delivered, which is a different question.

questions.prompt: A manager at Ivel Pharma proposes using the value stream map to rank teams by their process time. What is the best response?

options.text: Decline, since maps should stay with the facilitator
Agree, since ranking teams against each other creates healthy competition
Use the map to improve the system, since most delay sits between steps
Agree, but rank by lead time in place of process time

questions.explanation: The map is a tool for improving the whole stream, and the largest delays are usually in handoffs that no single team owns. Ranking teams pushes them to optimise locally and hide problems.

questions.prompt: A step at Dovecote Insurance has percent complete and accurate of 40. What does that suggest?

options.text: It uses less than half of its available capacity
Most of its output returns for clarification or correction
It finishes less than half of its planned work
It takes more than twice its estimated time

questions.explanation: A low value means the next step cannot use most of the work as received, which drives rework loops. It does not describe how much of the plan was finished.

questions.prompt: Which idea from Lean thinking does mapping serve most directly?

options.text: Centralise decisions to reduce variation
Maximise the utilisation of each specialist
Complete each phase in full before the next begins
Identify the value stream, then make value flow

questions.explanation: Lean thinking asks organisations to identify the value stream for each product and then make value flow. High utilisation of specialists creates queues, which is what the map tends to expose.

questions.prompt: The DevOps health radar at Kestrel Bank shows low scores for monitoring and for responding. Which pipeline aspect holds both?

options.text: Continuous Integration
Continuous Deployment
Continuous Exploration
Release on Demand

questions.explanation: Monitor and respond are two of the four activities of Continuous Deployment, after deploy and verify. Release on Demand contains stabilise, which sounds similar, but its four activities are release, stabilise, measure and learn.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps of a value stream mapping exercise in order.

options.text: Agree the scope of the stream, from trigger to delivered value
Record process time, lead time and percent complete and accurate
List the steps and who performs each
Design the future state and the improvement backlog
Total the metrics and find the largest delays

questions.explanation: The group scopes the stream, lays out the steps, adds the data, analyses it and then designs improvements. Jumping to improvements before the data is on the map leads to fixing the loudest complaint, not the largest delay.

questions.prompt: What does Continuous Exploration produce for the train?

options.text: A detailed requirements specification
A vision, a roadmap and a set of features
A release plan approved by operations
A tested build ready for staging

questions.explanation: Continuous Exploration aligns the train on what to build through a vision, a roadmap and features in the ART Backlog. A detailed specification written up front is the waterfall habit this aspect replaces.

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Continuous Exploration?

options.text: Release to customers, stabilize, measure, learn from feedback
Hypothesize, collaborate and research, architect, synthesize
Deploy to production, verify, monitor, respond and recover
Develop, build and integrate, test end-to-end, stage for deployment

questions.explanation: The study guide lists hypotheses, collaboration and research, architecting and synthesis for this aspect. The other three sets belong to integration, deployment and release on demand.

questions.prompt: A product manager at Ardent Payments treats a customer request as a confirmed requirement and schedules it. How does Continuous Exploration view the request?

options.text: As a commitment the train must now honour
As a hypothesis that still needs to be validated
As a defect in the current solution
As an enabler for the next planning interval

questions.explanation: SAFe treats ideas as hypotheses to validate through research and small experiments. Scheduling the request as a commitment skips the learning that shows whether it delivers the benefit expected.

questions.prompt: What is a benefit hypothesis?

options.text: The acceptance tests that prove a story is done
The proposed measurable benefit of a backlog item
The business benefit case signed off for an epic
The estimated cost of building a feature

questions.explanation: A benefit hypothesis states the measurable business or customer benefit an epic, capability, feature or story is expected to deliver. It is a claim to test, which is why a signed-off business case is the wrong picture.

questions.prompt: What is a Minimum Viable Product in SAFe?

options.text: A prototype shown to executives for funding
The first release that includes all planned features
An early, minimal version used to test an epic hypothesis
The smallest release that customers will pay for

questions.explanation: SAFe defines the MVP as an early and minimal version of a solution used to prove or disprove the epic hypothesis. The smallest sellable release is closer to a minimum marketable feature, which serves a different purpose.

questions.prompt: The MVP for an epic at Solace Health shows that clinics do not use the new booking flow. What should happen?

options.text: Increase the budget so adoption can catch up
Pivot or stop, since the hypothesis was not supported
Hide the result until the next portfolio review
Complete the remaining features as planned

questions.explanation: Lean startup thinking uses the MVP result to decide whether to persevere, pivot or stop. Finishing the plan regardless is the sunk-cost response the hypothesis-driven approach is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: Which measure would serve as a leading indicator for a hypothesis that a new checkout raises annual revenue at Juniper Outdoor?

options.text: The number of stories completed for the checkout
The team's velocity across the planning interval
The share of baskets that reach payment this week
The annual revenue reported next year

questions.explanation: A leading indicator is an early, measurable signal that predicts the business outcome. Annual revenue is the lagging result, and completed stories measure output with no link to customer behaviour.

questions.prompt: What is innovation accounting used for?

options.text: Recording hours spent on the IP iteration
Allocating the innovation budget across trains
Judging a hypothesis with early, actionable measures
Capitalising the cost of software development

questions.explanation: Innovation accounting uses leading indicators to evaluate a hypothesis long before financial results arrive. It sounds like a finance practice, but it is a learning tool from Lean startup.

questions.prompt: Who should Product Management involve during exploration?

options.text: Customers, business owners, architects and Agile teams
The portfolio office and no one from the teams
The marketing group, after features are defined
The operations group, once deployment begins

questions.explanation: The exploration article names customers, suppliers, partners, business owners, Agile teams and others as stakeholders. Leaving the teams out until features are defined loses their knowledge of what is feasible.

questions.prompt: A product manager at Wren Logistics wants to learn how dispatchers work. Which approach gives primary research?

options.text: Compare the feature lists of two competitors
Read an analyst report on the logistics market
Review last year's support ticket categories
Spend a day watching them at their desks

questions.explanation: Primary research gathers first-hand evidence, for example by observing users where they work. Analyst reports and competitor comparisons are secondary research, useful but one step removed.

questions.prompt: What does Lean UX emphasise?

options.text: Pixel-level sign-off by stakeholders
A separate design phase for each feature
Complete design before development
Iterative learning and customer outcomes

questions.explanation: SAFe describes Lean UX as a team-based approach that focuses on iterative learning, overall experience and customer outcomes over a theoretically ideal design. Designing everything first delays the feedback it relies on.

questions.prompt: A train at Greyfell Bank wants to deploy daily but its services share one database schema that needs a coordinated change for each feature. Which exploration activity addresses this?

options.text: Collaborate and research
Architect
Hypothesize
Synthesize

questions.explanation: The architect activity shapes the solution for continuous delivery, including the runway that lets features flow with little redesign. Synthesize turns the ideas into backlog features and comes after this thinking.

questions.prompt: What is the Architectural Runway?

options.text: A long-range plan for replacing the legacy systems across the portfolio
Existing code, components and infrastructure for near-term features
The list of approved technology standards
A reserved iteration for architecture work

questions.explanation: The runway is the existing code, components and technical infrastructure needed to implement near-term features with minimal redesign and delay. It is something that exists, not a plan or a standards list.

questions.prompt: A train at Petrel Media relies on emergent design alone across twelve teams. Which problem does SAFe expect?

options.text: Slower teams because of central approval
Too much documentation of design decisions
One-off solutions that are hard to change and reuse
Features that are too small to demonstrate

questions.explanation: The runway article says that at scale, emergent design alone leads to missing standards, one-off solutions and poor interoperability. Central approval is a risk of the opposite extreme, heavy up-front design.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe balance design at scale?

options.text: It replaces emergent design with a central blueprint
It leaves all design to each team's judgement
It combines emergent design with intentional architecture
It fixes the architecture before the first interval

questions.explanation: SAFe pairs emergent design with intentional architecture, which adds planning and coordination across teams. Replacing emergence with a blueprint returns to big design up front.

questions.prompt: What is an enabler?

options.text: A feature requested by an internal customer
A team member who removes impediments for the train during an interval
A tool that automates part of the pipeline
A backlog item that extends the runway or improves the value stream

questions.explanation: Enablers are backlog items that extend the Architectural Runway or improve the performance of the development value stream. They are work items, so they are estimated, prioritised and demonstrated like any other.

questions.prompt: A train at Marlow Energy needs a new automated test environment. Which type of enabler is this?

options.text: Compliance
Architecture
Infrastructure
Exploration

questions.explanation: Infrastructure enablers create and improve development and runtime environments. Architecture enablers build the runway in the solution itself, which is close but concerns components and design.

questions.prompt: A team at Sable Insurance must automate evidence for a regulatory audit. Which enabler type fits?

options.text: Compliance
Infrastructure
Exploration
Architecture

questions.explanation: Compliance enablers cover verification and validation, audits and approvals, and policy automation. Infrastructure is tempting because automation is involved, but the purpose here is meeting a regulation.

questions.prompt: What are nonfunctional requirements?

options.text: Requirements that were rejected by the business as too costly
System qualities that guide design and act as constraints
Features that have no visible user interface
Tasks that support a story but add no value

questions.explanation: NFRs are system qualities such as security, performance and scalability that guide the design and often constrain the backlogs. They are not a kind of feature without a screen.

questions.prompt: A team at Hollin Rail adds a performance requirement to a single story and forgets it afterwards. Why is that a weak way to handle an NFR?

options.text: An NFR is tested once by the System Team, at the end of the planning interval
An NFR belongs to the architect and not to teams
An NFR must be written as a separate feature
An NFR constrains many items and is checked again in each increment

questions.explanation: NFRs act as constraints across backlogs and are revisited as part of the definition of done for each iteration, interval or release. Treating one as a single story lets later work break it unnoticed.

questions.prompt: During exploration at Tarn Systems, an architect insists on feature toggles and backward-compatible interfaces. What is the architect designing for?

options.text: Compliance, so audits take less effort
Usability, so customers need less training
Releasability, so deployment and release can be separated
Capacity, so several teams can work on one component in parallel

questions.explanation: Toggles and compatible interfaces let code reach production without changing behaviour until the business chooses to release. This is a design decision, which is why it starts in exploration and not at deployment time.

questions.prompt: A security specialist at Elmfield Bank joins exploration to identify how a new payment feature could be attacked. Which practice is this?

options.text: Penetration testing
Threat modelling
Chaos engineering
Static code analysis

questions.explanation: Threat modelling examines a design for possible attacks before code is written, which is why it sits in the architect activity. Penetration testing needs a running system and happens later.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a feature is correct in SAFe?

options.text: It needs portfolio approval and a Lean business case before work starts
It is a technical task that supports a story
It delivers business value and fits within one planning interval
It fits within one iteration for a single team

questions.explanation: A feature is solution functionality that delivers business value, meets a stakeholder need and is sized for one train in one planning interval. The portfolio approval and Lean business case belong to epics.

questions.prompt: Exploration at Dunmore Travel has produced validated ideas. What does the synthesize activity do with them?

options.text: Deploys them to staging so they appear in the next system demo
Hands them to operations as change requests
Commits them to version control as stories
Shapes them into prioritised features in the ART Backlog

questions.explanation: Synthesize turns the understanding gained into a vision, a roadmap and prioritised features ready for PI Planning. Committing work to version control is the develop activity in Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: How is Weighted Shortest Job First calculated?

options.text: Job size divided by cost of delay
Business value multiplied by job size
Cost of delay divided by job size
Cost of delay added to job size

questions.explanation: WSJF divides the cost of delay by the job size, so valuable, short jobs come first. Inverting the fraction would favour the largest and least urgent work.

questions.prompt: Which three parts make up the cost of delay in WSJF?

options.text: User-business value, time criticality, risk reduction or opportunity enablement
Development cost, testing cost and the operating cost over the first three years
Revenue, market share, customer satisfaction
Story points, team capacity, iteration length

questions.explanation: Cost of delay adds user and business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement. Development and testing costs relate to the job size, which is the denominator.

questions.prompt: Two backlog items at Corran Health have the same cost of delay. Item A is a 3 in size and item B is an 8. Which goes first under WSJF?

options.text: Item B, since the larger job delivers more value
Neither, since equal cost of delay means a tie
Item B, since large items should start early
Item A, since the smaller job gives a higher score

questions.explanation: With equal cost of delay, the smaller job has the higher WSJF score and delivers its value sooner. Starting the larger job first delays both.

questions.prompt: A pipeline automation enabler at Lyle Telecom has a higher WSJF score than a customer feature. A stakeholder says customer features come first. What does SAFe economics say?

options.text: Sequence by WSJF, since the enabler has the better return
Sequence the enabler last, since it has no user value
Sequence the feature first, since enablers are overhead
Split capacity evenly, whatever the scores say

questions.explanation: WSJF applies to the whole backlog, and an enabler that removes delay from each later feature can carry a high cost of delay. Treating enablers as overhead leaves the pipeline slow and makes every feature more expensive.

questions.prompt: A product manager at Varley Foods writes a full requirements document for the year before any team sees it. Which exploration idea does this conflict with?

options.text: A vision that stays stable for the year
A roadmap that shows committed dates for the next four quarters
A fixed scope agreed with business owners
A steady flow of small features that give fast feedback

questions.explanation: Continuous Exploration replaces large up-front requirements with a continuous flow of features that are split into small stories. A year of fixed requirements delays feedback until it is expensive to act on.

questions.prompt: Match each enabler type to its work.

options.text: Verification, audits and policy automation
Building the Architectural Runway
Research and prototyping to understand options
Marketing a released feature
Improving development and runtime environments

questions.explanation: The four enabler types are exploration, architecture, infrastructure and compliance. Marketing a feature is a release activity and not an enabler type.

questions.prompt: Put the four activities of Continuous Exploration in order.

options.text: Collaborate and research
Hypothesize
Architect
Synthesize

questions.explanation: Exploration starts with a hypothesis, tests it through collaboration and research, shapes the architecture and then synthesizes the result into features. Synthesize comes last because it needs the outputs of the other three.

questions.prompt: What happens in Continuous Integration?

options.text: Functionality is made available to chosen customers
Validated and integrated changes move from staging to production
New functionality is developed, tested, integrated and validated
Customer needs are researched and turned into features

questions.explanation: Continuous Integration is the pipeline aspect where functionality is developed, tested, integrated and validated ready for deployment. Moving changes from staging to production is Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Continuous Integration?

options.text: Deploy, verify, monitor, respond
Plan, code, review, merge
Build, deploy, release, measure
Develop, build, test end-to-end, stage

questions.explanation: The integration article lists develop, build, test end-to-end and stage. Deploy, verify, monitor and respond are the activities of Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: What does the build activity produce?

options.text: A production release for early customers
Deployable binaries, with branches merged into the trunk
Stories that are committed to version control
A staging environment that mirrors production in each detail

questions.explanation: Build creates deployable binaries and merges development branches into the trunk. Committing stories to version control belongs to the develop activity that precedes it.

questions.prompt: Engineers at Farrow Systems keep feature branches open for three weeks, and merges fail often. Which practice helps most?

options.text: A dedicated integrator who merges for the teams
Longer branches with a final review board
Trunk-based development with frequent small merges
A merge freeze until the end of the interval

questions.explanation: Short-lived branches merged into the trunk at least daily keep integration problems small. A dedicated integrator moves the pain to one person and leaves the batch size as large as before.

questions.prompt: A change at Pell Digital breaks the main line for the whole train. Which practice would have stopped it reaching the trunk?

options.text: A weekly review of all the changes merged into the trunk
A rule that senior developers approve each merge by hand
A gated commit that runs the build and tests first
A larger staging environment

questions.explanation: Gated commits validate a change with an automated build and tests before it is merged into the trunk. A weekly review finds the break after everyone has already been blocked.

questions.prompt: A train at Osprey Rail integrates hardware and software from a supplier, and full integration is costly. What does SAFe advise?

options.text: Balance integration frequency, scope and testing cost
Integrate hourly whatever the cost
Exclude the supplier's parts from integration
Integrate once, shortly before the release date

questions.explanation: The integration article says such systems need an approach that balances frequency, the scope of integration and testing cost. Integrating once before release defers all the risk to the worst moment.

questions.prompt: During development at Halcyon Pay, the main line is often broken for days. Which integration principle is being missed?

options.text: The system should be running and potentially deployable throughout
The system should be rebuilt at the end of each interval
The system should be frozen before each demo
The system should be integrated by the System Team before each demo

questions.explanation: SAFe says the system should always run and be potentially deployable, even during development. Relying on the System Team to integrate makes integration someone else's job and delays feedback.

questions.prompt: A developer at Cobalt Travel writes a failing unit test, then the code to pass it, then tidies the design. Which practice is this?

options.text: Test-Driven Development
Behavior-Driven Development
Exploratory testing
Regression testing

questions.explanation: TDD builds and runs the test before the code it checks, then refactors. BDD also works test-first, but it specifies business-facing behaviour in scenarios.

questions.prompt: A product owner, a developer and a tester at Linden Health agree examples of how a refund should behave before coding starts. Which practice is this?

options.text: Pair programming
Test-Driven Development
Exploratory testing after each iteration
Behavior-Driven Development

questions.explanation: BDD creates shared understanding through business-facing scenarios defined before or with the specification of behaviour, using customer, development and test perspectives. TDD is the developer-level cycle on units of code.

questions.prompt: What mix of tests does a test-first approach tend to produce?

options.text: Many manual end-to-end tests and few unit tests
Few tests of any kind, written after release
Equal numbers of unit tests, integration tests and manual checks at each level
Many fast automated developer tests and fewer slow end-to-end tests

questions.explanation: Writing tests first gives a large base of fast automated tests and a smaller number of slow end-to-end ones, the shape of the testing pyramid. A suite that is mostly manual and end-to-end is slow and makes daily integration impractical.

questions.prompt: End-to-end tests at Thorne Bank fail because a partner's payment service is rarely available in test. Which technique helps?

options.text: Skipping payment tests until the partner is ready
Testing the payment flow in production alone
Asking the partner service team to pause its releases
Service virtualisation that simulates the partner service

questions.explanation: Service virtualisation stands in for systems that are unavailable or expensive to use, so end-to-end tests can run continuously. Skipping the tests removes feedback on one of the riskiest flows.

questions.prompt: Tests pass before deployment at Rook Media but the same build fails when live. Which gap should the train close first?

options.text: Differences between test and production environments
Differences between story and feature estimates
Differences in the skills of testers and developers
Differences in the length of iterations

questions.explanation: Test results are trustworthy when test environments resemble production in configuration and data. Environment drift is a common reason a build that passed still fails once deployed.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the stage activity?

options.text: To collect usage data from customers
To host and validate the solution before production
To merge feature branches into the trunk
To release the solution to a first group of users

questions.explanation: Stage hosts and validates the solution in a staging environment before it goes to production. Releasing to a first group of users is a release decision, made after deployment.

questions.prompt: A train at Mistral Insurance keeps two identical production environments and switches traffic between them. Which technique is this?

options.text: Blue-green deployment
Canary release to early users
Feature toggle
Dark launch

questions.explanation: Blue-green deployment keeps an idle environment for the new version and switches traffic when it is ready, which also gives a fast way back. A canary release exposes the change to a small share of users first.

questions.prompt: A team at Ember Logistics stores application code in version control but keeps server configuration on a shared drive. What is the risk?

options.text: The trunk will hold too many small changes to review
Environments cannot be rebuilt reliably or audited
The System Demo will take longer
Developers will commit too frequently to the trunk each day

questions.explanation: Everything needed to build, test and deploy belongs in version control, including configuration and scripts. Without that, nobody can reproduce an environment or trace what changed before a failure.

questions.prompt: Where does the train see integrated work from all teams each iteration?

options.text: At the PO Sync
At each team's iteration retrospective
At the Inspect and Adapt workshop alone
At the System Demo

questions.explanation: The System Demo shows the integrated work of all teams on the train, usually from a staging environment. Inspect and Adapt includes a demo too, but it happens once per planning interval.

questions.prompt: A team at Quill Bank wants to add static security analysis. Where in the pipeline does it give the fastest feedback?

options.text: In staging, once per interval
In the build, on each commit
In production, after release
In a review before the annual audit

questions.explanation: Automated scanning in the build tells the developer about a weakness minutes after writing it. Leaving it to staging or an audit lets vulnerable code spread before anyone knows.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for quality on an Agile team practising agile testing?

options.text: The testers on the team
The product owner
The System Team
The whole team

questions.explanation: Agile testing is collaborative, and all team members share responsibility for quality. Assigning it to testers alone brings back the handoff from developers to a test phase.

questions.prompt: Put the four activities of Continuous Integration in order.

options.text: Test end-to-end
Develop
Stage
Build

questions.explanation: Work is developed, built, tested end-to-end and then staged. Stage comes last because it validates the tested solution in a production-like environment before deployment.

questions.prompt: What does Continuous Deployment do?

options.text: Makes new functionality visible to all customers
Automates moving functionality from staging to production
Decides which features customers will receive
Integrates code from all teams into the trunk

questions.explanation: Continuous Deployment automates the migration of functionality from staging into production, where it becomes available for release. Making it visible to customers is a separate release decision.

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Continuous Deployment?

options.text: Release, stabilize, measure, learn
Stage, deploy, release, support
Develop, build, test end-to-end, stage
Deploy, verify, monitor, respond

questions.explanation: The deployment article lists deploy, verify, monitor and respond. Release, stabilize, measure and learn belong to Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe separate deployment from release?

options.text: Developers can skip testing in the staging environment
Releases can be bundled into fewer, larger events
Changes can reach production without changing what users see
Operations can approve each change before it is built

questions.explanation: With deployment separate from release, functionality sits in production, verified, until the business chooses to turn it on. Bundling releases into larger events is the opposite of the small batches this enables.

questions.prompt: A team at Aldous Retail deploys a new pricing engine to production but keeps it switched off for customers. Which technique allows this?

options.text: A blue-green switch of all traffic
A gated commit
A rollback
A feature toggle

questions.explanation: A feature toggle lets deployed code stay hidden until it is switched on, for everyone or for chosen users. A blue-green switch changes the whole environment and does not hide one feature inside it.

questions.prompt: At Sorrel Bank, a new fraud model runs in production on live traffic, and its results are recorded but not used. What is this called?

options.text: A dark launch
A system demo
A hotfix
A canary release

questions.explanation: A dark launch puts functionality into production without exposing it to users, so the team can see how it behaves under real conditions. A canary release does expose the change, to a small group of users.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the verify activity?

options.text: To confirm the business owners approve the release
To confirm the build compiles without warnings
To confirm changes work in production before customers see them
To confirm stories meet their acceptance criteria in test

questions.explanation: Verify checks that changes operate in production as intended before they are released to customers. Checking acceptance criteria in a test environment happens earlier, in integration.

questions.prompt: Which practice supports the verify activity?

options.text: Automated production tests run after each deployment
A weekly meeting of the change board
A user acceptance phase held before the staging environment
A survey sent to customers after release

questions.explanation: Automated tests in production confirm that the deployed change behaves correctly in its real environment. A change board meeting adds delay and tells nobody whether the change works.

questions.prompt: What does the monitor activity cover?

options.text: Auditing commits for coding standards
Reviewing features with the business owners
Tracking team velocity across iterations
Watching production and reporting on issues

questions.explanation: Monitor means observing the production environment and reporting on any issues. It concerns the health of the running solution, not the progress of the teams.

questions.prompt: Operations at Tidewater Energy see server metrics, but nobody can tell whether a new feature is being used. What is missing?

options.text: Full-stack telemetry that includes business measures
A longer period of testing in staging
A larger operations team on each shift
A second monitoring tool for the servers and the network

questions.explanation: Full-stack telemetry collects data from infrastructure up to feature usage and business results, so technical and business questions can both be answered. A second server tool repeats the view the train already has.

questions.prompt: What does the respond activity mean?

options.text: Addressing problems rapidly when they occur
Replying to audit findings each quarter
Reporting status to the portfolio
Answering customer feature requests

questions.explanation: Respond is the ability to address problems rapidly when they arise in deployment and production. It is about incidents, not about requests for new functionality.

questions.prompt: A deployment at Garnet Travel causes errors for a tenth of users. The team can undo the change in two minutes or write a fix in about an hour. Which reasoning fits?

options.text: Leave the change live and fix it within the hour
Wait for the next planned deployment window
Call a change board to decide the next step
Roll back now to restore service, then fix the cause

questions.explanation: Restoring service fast is the priority, and a two-minute rollback does that while the team works on the cause. Fixing forward is reasonable when it is quicker or rollback is unsafe, which is not the case here.

questions.prompt: Servers at Bexley Insurance are patched by hand and have drifted apart, so deployments behave differently on each. Which practice removes the drift?

options.text: Immutable infrastructure rebuilt from versioned definitions
A monthly meeting to compare settings
A detailed manual that describes the settings of each server
A freeze on changes to the servers

questions.explanation: With immutable infrastructure, servers are replaced from definitions held in version control and are never changed in place, so each one matches. A manual describes the intended state but cannot enforce it.

questions.prompt: A train at Larch Pay deploys by hand once a month. Leaders say automation is too costly. Which economic argument does SAFe make?

options.text: Automation pays back when releases become larger
Automation removes the need for monitoring
Automation lowers transaction cost, so small batches pay off
Automation raises quality so far that staging tests can be dropped

questions.explanation: The deployment article says teams reduce the transaction cost and risk of moving changes to production by automating, which makes small batches worthwhile. Automation does not replace testing or monitoring; it makes them repeatable.

questions.prompt: A product manager at Onyx Media wants to compare two versions of a sign-up page with real users. What makes this possible?

options.text: A manual switch performed during a change window
A longer staging period, so both versions are tested by the whole train
Deployment separated from release, so each group sees one version
A second production release, scheduled for next month

questions.explanation: Separating deployment from release allows experiments such as A/B tests, because functionality can be shown to chosen users. Staging has no real customers, so it cannot answer which version they prefer.

questions.prompt: Developers at Finch Health must raise a ticket and wait two days for operations to deploy to a test environment. Which practice removes the queue?

options.text: A form with more detail on each request
A weekly slot reserved for test deployments
A second operations engineer assigned to handle the tickets
Self-service deployment through the automated pipeline

questions.explanation: Self-service deployment lets teams trigger a controlled, automated deployment themselves, which removes the wait. Another engineer shortens the queue for a while but keeps the handoff.

questions.prompt: An incident review at Wexford Bank ends by naming the engineer who ran the failed command. What is wrong with that outcome?

options.text: It leaves out the cost of the incident
It should have been decided by the change board, not the team
It hides the system causes and discourages open reporting
It should also name the engineer's manager

questions.explanation: A blameless review looks for the conditions that allowed the failure, so the system can be improved. Naming a person teaches people to conceal problems, which slows detection next time.

questions.prompt: Which practice lets a train send a change to one region before the rest?

options.text: Service virtualisation
Trunk-based development
Selective deployment
Gated commit

questions.explanation: Selective deployment sends a change to specific environments or segments first, which limits the effect of a problem. The other options are integration practices that act before deployment.

questions.prompt: A team at Ridgeway Rail notices rising memory use and replaces the instance before users are affected. Which capability is this?

options.text: Proactive detection
Dark launch
Session replay
Canary release

questions.explanation: Proactive detection finds problems before they cause an outage, often through telemetry and deliberate fault testing. Session replay helps to understand a problem after a user has already met it.

questions.prompt: Put the four activities of Continuous Deployment in order.

options.text: Verify
Deploy
Monitor
Respond

questions.explanation: The solution is deployed, verified in production, monitored and then problems are responded to. Verify precedes monitor because the team first confirms the change works before watching it over time.

questions.prompt: What is Release on Demand?

options.text: Releasing each change to all customers as soon as it passes its last test
Releasing all features at the end of a planning interval
Releasing functionality at once or in increments, as the business needs
Releasing when operations has capacity to support it

questions.explanation: Release on Demand makes functionality available immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs. Releasing each change the moment it passes tests ignores the business decision about timing.

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Release on Demand?

options.text: Deploy, verify, monitor, respond
Stage, release, monitor, improve
Release, stabilize, measure, learn
Plan, release, support, retire

questions.explanation: The study guide lists releasing value, stabilising the solution, measuring business value and learning from feedback. Deploy, verify, monitor and respond are the deployment activities that come before.

questions.prompt: Who decides when a feature is released to customers?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer with the System Team
Product Management with the business owners
The operations lead on call
The team that built the feature

questions.explanation: The release article says Product Management and business owners decide when to release, which features and to whom. The team makes deployment routine, but the timing of release is a business decision.

questions.prompt: A feature at Halyard Retail is deployed and verified in September, but marketing wants to launch it with a November campaign. What does SAFe allow?

options.text: Remove it from production until November
Delay all other deployments until November
Release it now, since it is ready
Keep it deployed and release it in November

questions.explanation: Because release is decoupled from deployment, the business can choose a release date that suits market rhythms and campaigns. Removing working code from production adds risk and gains nothing.

questions.prompt: A team at Pallas Bank shows a new transfer screen to two percent of customers and watches the error rate before widening it. Which technique is this?

options.text: A gated commit
A dark launch
A blue-green deployment
A canary release

questions.explanation: A canary release exposes a change to a small group of real users and expands as confidence grows. A dark launch runs in production without users seeing it at all.

questions.prompt: A solution at Seaton Telecom has a web front end, an API and a billing engine that are always released together. What would SAFe suggest?

options.text: Release the billing engine first and the rest a year later
Merge the three elements into one component
Decouple the elements so each can release independently
Give all three the cadence of the slowest element

questions.explanation: Decoupling release elements lets parts of the solution reach customers at the pace each market needs. Tying everything to the slowest element delays value that is ready now.

questions.prompt: What is the aim of the stabilize activity?

options.text: Freezing changes until the next planning interval
Reducing the number of features in the release
Completing the tests that were skipped earlier in the interval
Keeping the released solution reliable, secure and available

questions.explanation: Stabilize makes sure the solution keeps meeting its nonfunctional requirements in operation, with practices such as failover and continuous security monitoring. It is not a hardening phase for unfinished testing.

questions.prompt: A region fails at Kelso Health and traffic moves to a second region without users noticing. Which stabilize practice does this show?

options.text: Innovation accounting and leading indicators
Threat modelling
Feature toggles
Failover and disaster recovery

questions.explanation: Failover and disaster recovery are designed and rehearsed so the service survives the loss of a component or site. Threat modelling is a design-time security practice used in exploration.

questions.prompt: A feature at Briar Travel was released with the expectation that it would raise repeat bookings. What does the measure activity do?

options.text: Counts the story points the feature took
Compares actual results with the benefit hypothesis
Records how many defects were fixed
Confirms the feature passed its acceptance tests

questions.explanation: Measure evaluates whether the released functionality delivers the benefit that was predicted, using the indicators chosen during exploration. Passing acceptance tests shows the feature was built as specified, not that it was worth building.

questions.prompt: What happens to what the train learns after a release?

options.text: It is kept by Product Management until the next year
It is reported to operations for future support
It is archived with the release notes
It feeds back into Continuous Exploration

questions.explanation: The release article says the activities of Release on Demand feed back into exploration, which closes the loop of the pipeline. Archiving the learning breaks the loop and the next hypothesis starts from guesswork.

questions.prompt: Results at Morven Foods show a released feature has no effect on orders. Which options does Lean startup thinking offer?

options.text: Add more features until orders rise
Remove the measures that show no effect
Hand the feature to another train
Pivot, persevere with changes, or stop

questions.explanation: The learn activity uses the evidence to decide whether to pivot, persevere or stop. Adding features without a new hypothesis spends more on an idea the data has not supported.

questions.prompt: Leaders at Castell Insurance say release on demand means every team must release daily. What is the best correction?

options.text: Release frequency follows the length of the iteration
Release frequency is fixed at once per planning interval for each train
Release frequency follows business need, which differs by solution
Release frequency is set by the slowest team

questions.explanation: On demand means the business can release when it wants to, whether that is many times a day or a few times a year. The planning interval is a cadence for planning and does not dictate release timing.

questions.prompt: What does decoupling release from deployment give the sales and marketing groups?

options.text: Control of the team backlog
Confidence to schedule launches and promotions
Access to the staging environment
The authority to approve or reject each deployment

questions.explanation: The release article notes that decoupling lets marketing target promotions and sales schedule with confidence. They gain predictability of release timing, not a role in approving deployments.

questions.prompt: After a release at Ostrander Pay, the team runs a value stream mapping session on its own pipeline. Which activity is this part of?

options.text: Verify
Learn
Stabilize
Release

questions.explanation: Learn includes relentless improvement of the pipeline itself, and mapping the value stream again shows where the next delay sits. Stabilize keeps the running solution healthy and does not examine the delivery process.

questions.prompt: Match each activity to its aspect of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

options.text: Continuous Integration
Continuous Deployment
Value Stream Mapping
Release on Demand
Continuous Exploration

questions.explanation: Synthesize ends exploration, stage ends integration, verify follows deploy, and stabilize follows release. Value stream mapping is a technique for improving the pipeline and is not one of its four aspects.
